paras: The lynching of Sam Fields was the killing of a young Black man by a mob of white men in Livingston Parish, Louisiana, in August 1900. Fields was accused of attempting to assault a white woman, Mrs. Poche, and was shot to death, either after a posse chased him into the swamps or after a mob took him from officers. The killing reached papers across the country through New Orleans wire dispatches, but no coverage was found in the Black press.

The first report, a special to the New-York Tribune, placed the episode at Island, which it called an out-of-the-way corner of Livingstone Parish. According to that dispatch, the news reached New Orleans by a small steamer to Manchac and then by railroad, and few details could be obtained.

Fields was accused of entering a farmhouse and attacking a white woman who was alone, named as Mrs. Joseph Poche in one wire and Mrs. Peter Poche in the Associated Press version. The reports said she resisted until help arrived, and a later dispatch said that through her 'desperate resistance' he had not succeeded.

In the first dispatches, dated Aug. 21, Fields fled into the swamps pursued by 'a posse of white men' and was caught at New River Bridge, or near Old River Bridge. There, the Sun's wire said, he 'was riddled with bullets and the body thrown into Bayou Manchac'; the Tribune added that he was killed 'without the formality of the accustomed rope.'

An Associated Press dispatch dated Aug. 23 gave a different account, saying Fields was shot to death 'last night' near Whitehall. In that version the woman reported the attempt, Fields was captured, and officers were taking him by buggy to the county seat at Somerville when a mob surrounded the buggy, took him 'forcibly from the officers' and shot him.
The Associated Press reported that 'the parish is entirely quiet to-day.' No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no member of the mob was named.

The story ran only in white papers, first in New York and Alexandria on Aug. 22 and then, in the Associated Press version, in dailies from Wheeling and Indianapolis to St. Louis on Aug. 24. Reprints followed in Salt Lake City, Butte, Portland, Raleigh and Savannah, then in weeklies in Oregon, Wisconsin, South Dakota, Minnesota and Michigan, and in the Hawaiian Star on Sept. 4.

Most papers printed the item in two or three sentences, stating the alleged assault as fact, under headlines such as 'Negro Shot to Death' and 'Mob Killed a Negro.' The Wheeling Register went further, headlining it 'Negro Who Attempted to Outrage a White Woman Promtly Lynched.' Other headlines treated it as one in a series, among them the Salt Lake Herald's 'Another Negro Lynched' and the Hawaiian Star's 'The Daily Lynching.'
No account of the killing was found in the Black press, including the Richmond Planet's weekly news column for Aug. 25.

The two wire versions differ on the victim's first name, Sam or Samuel Fields against 'Joe Field', and on the woman's name. They also differ on the date: the Aug. 21 dispatch said the killing happened 'yesterday' and the Alexandria Gazette said 'Monday', while the Associated Press said 'last night' in an Aug. 23 dispatch, or 'Wednesday night'. Because the Tribune and Sun printed the killing on the morning of Aug. 22, the earlier date fits the publication record better.

The accounts also disagree on how Fields was taken: a posse chased him down at a river bridge in the first dispatches, while the later, more detailed Associated Press account has a mob seizing him from officers on the road to Somerville.

reader.title: Lynching of Sam Fields
bases: Every account describes a Black man accused of an attempted assault on a white woman being shot to death by a mob of white men, either after a posse pursuit (A1, A2) or after being taken from officers (A6, A8).

Both versions report Fields shot to death by 'a mob of white men' (A2, A4, A8), in one version after the mob took him forcibly from officers (A8, A16), in punishment for an alleged attempted assault on a white woman (A1, A16); the Tribune noted only that the 'accustomed rope' was omitted (A1).

Two separate New Orleans dispatches, a Tribune special (A1) and a wire (A2, A3), and a later AP report (A4, A8, A16) agree that a Black man named Fields was killed by a white mob in Livingston Parish after an alleged attempted assault on a Mrs. Poche, though they differ on date, place, first name and how he was taken.

accounts.label: First New Orleans dispatches (Aug. 21)
accounts.gist: News that came 'by a little steamer to Manchac' said Fields attacked a woman alone in a farmhouse, fled to the swamps pursued by a posse, and was caught at a river bridge, shot and thrown into the river or Bayou Manchac, on about Monday, Aug. 20.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire (Aug. 23-24)
accounts.gist: Fields was captured after the woman reported the attempt and was being taken by officers to Somerville in a buggy when a mob surrounded it, took him and shot him to death 'last night' / 'Wednesday night' near Whitehall.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP item in two or three sentences under headlines such as 'Negro Shot to Death' and 'Mob Killed a Negro', stating the alleged assault as fact.
The Wheeling Register headlined 'Negro Who Attempted to Outrage a White Woman Promtly Lynched', presenting the accusation as settled and the lynching as prompt.
The New-York Tribune's special noted the remote location and few details, and that he was shot 'without the formality of the accustomed rope'.
